First principles. What actually happens when you press the power button?
First, firmware wakes up. On modern machines, that's UEFI. Its only job is to find something it can boot.
lines.say: First, firmware wakes up. On modern machines, that's U E F I. Its only job is to find something it can boot.

lines.text: That something is a bootloader. The bootloader's only job is to load the kernel.
The kernel is the program that talks to your hardware, so that nothing else has to.
Then the kernel starts exactly one process: PID 1. On Arch, that's systemd. Every program you'll ever run descends from it.
lines.say: Then the kernel starts exactly one process: P I D one. On Arch, that's system D. Every program you'll ever run descends from it.

lines.text: Above that is userspace: shells, tools, desktops, games. And above that: you.
So it's a tech tree.
Exactly. Most distros unlock the whole tree for you. Arch hands you the skill points.

Step one: boot the live USB, and check that you're in UEFI mode.

Patience. First, some people have objections.
OBJECTION! First principles? You downloaded precompiled binaries! On Gentoo, we compile everything from source. With custom flags.

If first principles means building every byte yourself, Linux From Scratch wins. If it means reproducibility, NixOS has the stronger case.
lines.say: If first principles means building every byte yourself, Linux from Scratch wins. If it means reproducibility, Nix O S has the stronger case.

lines.text: Arch makes a narrower claim: it's the least abstraction you can have while still finishing before lunch. You see every layer, but you don't have to forge each one by hand.
My lunch has been compiling since Tuesday.
Citizen! The Arch Way rests on five official principles. Commit them to memory.
One: Simplicity!
Simple doesn't mean easy. It means software ships as its upstream developers released it, with as few distro-specific changes as possible.
Two: Modernity!
Arch is a rolling release. There's no big upgrade from version twelve to version thirteen, because there are no versions. There is only the update.
Three: Pragmatism!
Decisions are made on technical merit, not ideology. Want proprietary GPU drivers? They're in the repos.
lines.say: Decisions are made on technical merit, not ideology. Want proprietary G P U drivers? They're in the repos.

lines.text: Four: User centrality!
Arch isn't trying to be user-friendly. It's trying to be user-centric: built for people who want to understand and control their own system.
Five: Versatility!
Start from a minimal base and build it into anything. A server. A gaming rig. A laptop with forty-seven browser tabs open.
Forty-seven is actually low for me.
Arch's package manager is called pacman, and one command upgrades your entire system.
lines.say: Arch's package manager is called Pac-Man, and one command upgrades your entire system.

lines.text: Capital S means sync with the repositories. y refreshes the package database. u upgrades everything that's out of date.
lines.say: Capital S means sync with the repositories. Y refreshes the package database. U upgrades everything that's out of date.

lines.text: Here's the first-principles part. At any moment, the Arch repos are one consistent snapshot. Every package was built against the other packages in that same snapshot.
So if you refresh the database but only install one new package, it expects newer libraries than the ones you have. That's a partial upgrade. It's unsupported, and things break in fascinating ways.
So Arch doesn't break. I break Arch.
Usually. And occasionally an update needs manual intervention, which is why you check the news on archlinux.org before a big update.
lines.say: Usually. And occasionally an update needs manual intervention, which is why you check the news on arch linux dot org before a big update.

lines.text: Also: add ILoveCandy to pacman.conf, and the progress bar turns into a little yellow creature eating dots. This is a real feature. It's been there for years.
lines.say: Also: add I love candy to Pac-Man dot conf, and the progress bar turns into a little yellow creature eating dots. This is a real feature. It's been there for years.

lines.text: It's the most important line in my entire config.
The official repos are big. The Arch User Repository, the AUR, is bigger: tens of thousands of community-made packages.

lines.text: But an AUR package isn't a binary. It's a PKGBUILD: a small shell script that tells makepkg how to download, build, and package something.
lines.say: But an A U R package isn't a binary. It's a package build: a small shell script that tells make package how to download, build, and package something.

lines.text: Anyone can upload one. So, as a model with a professional interest in safety: please read the PKGBUILD before you build it.
lines.say: Anyone can upload one. So, as a model with a professional interest in safety: please read the package build before you build it.

lines.text: Okay. Propaganda over. Here's the real, step-by-step install for a brand-new computer, following the official Arch installation guide.
Pause whenever you need to. Every command stays on screen long enough to copy.
One warning before anything else: this erases the entire disk you install to. Back up anything you care about first.
You'll need a USB stick of at least 2 GB, a 64-bit UEFI computer, and an internet connection. Ethernet is easiest.
lines.say: You'll need a U S B stick of at least two gigabytes, a sixty four bit U E F I computer, and an internet connection. Ethernet is easiest.

lines.text: Socks on. Let's do it properly this time.
Step one: download the ISO and its signature from archlinux.org/download, then verify them. The download page lists the exact commands.
lines.say: Step one: download the I S O and its signature from arch linux dot org slash download, then verify them. The download page lists the exact commands.

lines.text: Step two: write it to the USB stick. On Linux, find the stick under /dev/disk/by-id, and copy the image onto the whole device, not a partition. On Windows, Rufus does the same job.
lines.say: Step two: write it to the U S B stick. On Linux, find the stick under slash dev slash disk slash by I D, and copy the image onto the whole device, not a partition. On Windows, Rufus does the same job.

lines.text: Step three: in the new computer's firmware settings, disable Secure Boot, because the install image doesn't support it. You can turn it back on later.
Then boot from the USB. Press the boot menu key shown on the startup screen, often F12, F11, F8, or Escape, and pick Arch Linux install medium.
lines.say: Then boot from the U S B. Press the boot menu key shown on the startup screen, often F twelve, F eleven, F eight, or Escape, and pick Arch Linux install medium.

lines.text: You're now at a root shell on the live system. If you don't use a US keyboard, set your layout with loadkeys. localectl list-keymaps shows every option.
lines.say: You're now at a root shell on the live system. If you don't use a U S keyboard, set your layout with load keys. Locale control list keymaps shows every option.

lines.text: Confirm UEFI mode. This should print 64. If it says no such file, you booted in legacy BIOS mode, so go back to the firmware settings.
lines.say: Confirm U E F I mode. This should print sixty four. If it says no such file, you booted in legacy BIOS mode, so go back to the firmware settings.

lines.text: Next, the network. Ethernet just works. For Wi-Fi, open iwctl, list your device, scan, and connect. Then ping to check.
lines.say: Next, the network. Ethernet just works. For Wi-Fi, open I W control, list your device, scan, and connect. Then ping to check.

lines.text: Finally, run timedatectl and check that the clock is synchronized. A wrong clock makes package signatures fail.
lines.say: Finally, run time date control and check that the clock is synchronized. A wrong clock makes package signatures fail.

lines.text: Find your disk with lsblk. An NVMe drive looks like nvme0n1, a SATA drive like sda. I'll use nvme0n1 from here on, so swap in your own name.
lines.say: Find your disk with L S B L K. An N V M E drive looks like N V M E zero N one, a SATA drive like S D A. I'll use N V M E zero N one from here on, so swap in your own name.

lines.text: Partition it with cfdisk. Choose GPT, then make three partitions: one gigabyte of type EFI System, at least four gigabytes of Linux swap, and the rest as the Linux root.
lines.say: Partition it with C F disk. Choose G P T, then make three partitions: one gigabyte of type E F I System, at least four gigabytes of Linux swap, and the rest as the Linux root.

lines.text: Choose Write, type yes, and quit.
Format them: FAT32 for the EFI partition, mkswap for the swap, and ext4 for root.
lines.say: Format them: fat thirty two for the E F I partition, make swap for the swap, and ext four for root.

lines.text: Then mount root on /mnt, mount the EFI partition on /mnt/boot, and switch the swap on.
lines.say: Then mount root on slash M N T, mount the E F I partition on slash M N T slash boot, and switch the swap on.

lines.text: Install the base system with pacstrap. Add your CPU's microcode, intel-ucode or amd-ucode, plus a network manager, sudo, a text editor, and the manual pages.
lines.say: Install the base system with pac strap. Add your C P U's microcode, Intel u code or A M D u code, plus a network manager, sudo, a text editor, and the manual pages.

lines.text: On a laptop, sof-firmware is often needed for the built-in speakers.
lines.say: On a laptop, S O F firmware is often needed for the built-in speakers.

lines.text: Generate the fstab so your partitions mount at every boot, and check that all three show up.
lines.say: Generate the F S tab so your partitions mount at every boot, and check that all three show up.

lines.text: Now step inside with arch-chroot dash capital S. The S runs it in systemd mode, which lets the bootloader installer register its boot entry later.
lines.say: Now step inside with arch change root, dash capital S. The S runs it in system D mode, which lets the bootloader installer register its boot entry later.

lines.text: Set your time zone, and write the hardware clock.
Uncomment your locale in /etc/locale.gen, for example en_US.UTF-8, run locale-gen, and put the same name in locale.conf.
lines.say: Uncomment your locale in slash etc slash locale dot gen, for example E N underscore U S dot U T F eight, run locale gen, and put the same name in locale dot conf.

lines.text: Give the machine a hostname, and set a root password.
Then create your everyday user in the wheel group, set its password, and run visudo to uncomment the one line that lets wheel use sudo.
lines.say: Then create your everyday user in the wheel group, set its password, and run V I sudo to uncomment the one line that lets wheel use sudo.

lines.text: Install systemd-boot onto the EFI partition.
lines.say: Install system D boot onto the E F I partition.

lines.text: Then write two small files. loader.conf picks the default entry. arch.conf says where the kernel and initramfs live, and which partition is root.
lines.say: Then write two small files. Loader dot conf picks the default entry. Arch dot conf says where the kernel and init ram F S live, and which partition is root.

lines.text: Don't type the root UUID by hand. Let blkid fill it in.
lines.say: Don't type the root U U I D by hand. Let B L K I D fill it in.

lines.text: You don't need a separate microcode line: the microcode is packed into the initramfs automatically.
lines.say: You don't need a separate microcode line: the microcode is packed into the init ram F S automatically.

lines.text: And enable NetworkManager, so the new system has internet on its first boot. The classic mistake. Not today.
lines.say: And enable Network Manager, so the new system has internet on its first boot. The classic mistake. Not today.

lines.text: Exit the chroot, unmount everything, and reboot. Pull out the USB stick when the screen goes dark.
lines.say: Exit the change root, unmount everything, and reboot. Pull out the U S B stick when the screen goes dark.

lines.text: Log in as your user. For Wi-Fi, nmtui gives you a simple menu. Update, then install a desktop: KDE Plasma, GNOME, or a tiling compositor like Hyprland.
lines.say: Log in as your user. For Wi-Fi, N M T U I gives you a simple menu. Update, then install a desktop: K D E Plasma, Gnome, or a tiling compositor like Hyper land.
